title: Choreography and Motion Mapping
answer: Kinematic generation, notation, motion capture retargeting, crowd simulation and biomechanics.

children.name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
children.blurb: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that turn recorded or synthetic motion into video, notation, or interactive choreography.

children.name: Dance Notation and Transcription
children.blurb: Dance notation and transcription in AI covers the conversion of human movement into structured, readable symbols or digital records, and the reverse process of turning a score back into motion.

children.name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
children.blurb: Motion capture and retargeting covers the recording of human or object movement and the transfer of that movement onto a digital skeleton or character.

children.name: Crowd and Ensemble Simulation
children.blurb: Crowd and ensemble simulation covers any scene where many bodies move at once and the interest lies in the group rather than the individual.

children.name: Biomechanical Analysis
children.blurb: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping examines how the human body moves under physical forces, using measurements such as joint angles, ground reaction forces, and muscle activity.

sections.body: Choreography and motion mapping is the part of AI work that deals with bodies moving through space and time, whether those bodies are real dancers, animated characters, or simulated crowds. In practice, systems now generate short kinematic sequences from text or music prompts, track performers with markerless pose estimation from ordinary video, and retarget motion from one skeleton to another so a routine captured on a human can drive a digital figure. Notation tools convert recorded movement into machine readable scores, and biomechanics pipelines measure joint angles, balance and force from the same capture data. None of this replaces a choreographer. It gives them faster drafts, searchable movement libraries and ways to test staging before anyone steps into a studio.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Motion capture and retargeting are the most mature areas, with reliable pipelines for cleaning data, solving skeletons and transferring motion between rigs of different proportions. Kinematic generation has improved quickly but remains fragile over long sequences, where drift, foot sliding and physically impossible transitions accumulate, and generated movement often reads as generic rather than authored. Dance notation is only partly solved, because Labanotation and Benesh were designed for human readers and their spatial and timing subtleties resist clean automation. Crowd simulation handles large numbers convincingly at a distance but struggles with individual intent and believable interaction. Biomechanical analysis is strong for measurement and weak for prediction, and any clinical or medical reading of its output belongs with qualified professionals, not with the software. The honest limit across the field is that models imitate the surface of movement well and understand its purpose poorly.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with Kinematic Video and Generated Movement for the generative side, meaning how text, audio or reference footage becomes a moving sequence and where those sequences break down. Dance Notation and Transcription covers the symbolic layer, the attempt to turn movement into a durable, searchable score and the reasons that translation is imperfect. Motion Capture and Retargeting is the practical engineering core, explaining how performance is recorded, cleaned and mapped onto new characters or robots. Crowd and Ensemble Simulation widens the frame from one body to many, dealing with group behaviour, spacing and the choreographic problems that appear only at scale. Biomechanical Analysis grounds all of it in measurement, offering the joint level and force level view that tells you whether a movement is physically plausible. Read together, the five pages move from generation to notation to capture to crowds to physical validation, which is roughly the order a production would follow.
